amendments.rule: Where English fuses several morphemes into one word, such as *wherein*, they share a unit **only when that shared English rendering carries the sense of every morpheme placed in it**. Reserve `added` for English that no morpheme licenses at all. This governs a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression the ASV renders with one English word too, but it never absorbs a morpheme whose sense that rendering does not carry: in `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles*, the two lexical nouns may share *chronicles*, while the separately segmented article takes a written *the* or is its own `unrepresented` unit; `אִם לֹא` → *surely* may share one unit when *surely* carries both morphemes' senses. Such a fused expression is headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, rather than leaving another morpheme whose sense the rendering carries `unrepresented`. The one-English-word condition is load-bearing in both directions: `בְּיַד` → *by* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* fuse, but where the ASV spends a second English word on the expression — `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses while the same idiom as *say ... nay* does not — the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. **Read that condition as one English rendering, not one English token.** A compound English preposition written in two or three words — *because of*, *by reason of*, *out of* — is a single rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and it fuses; so does an expression whose unit additionally carries a copula or other word the construction hands to the whole of it under another rule, as `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*. What defeats the condition is English the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so that each morpheme has a rendering of its own: `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives *to* to the preposition and *meet* to `פָּנֶה`, and `עַד לְ` → *until there was* gives *until* to `עַד` and the predicate's supplied copula to the `לְ` under rule 49, while the same `עַד לְ` → *to* fuses. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the second English word and ask whether a particular morpheme has lost its rendering or only the expression as a whole is diminished. What the second morpheme is tagged does not matter; a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition. **And such a compound's single English word carries the preposition's own relation even where no part of it states that relation separately.** Where `מִן`, `לְ`, `בְּ` or `עַל` stands before a construct noun and the ASV writes one English preposition for the pair, the condition is met and the two share a unit headed on the construct noun: `מִפְּנֵי` → *before*, `לִפְנֵי` → *before*, `עַל־פְּנֵי` → *upon*, `בְּקֶרֶב` → *among*. Do not read this rule's first sentence as requiring a separate English trace of the ablative, directional or locative sense before fusing, and do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` beside a construct noun holding the whole word: that is the outcome the fusion sentence above forbids and the one rule 22's closing paragraph forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a word, and the subtraction test finds no second English word for either morpheme to own. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `מִפְּנֵי` → *from before*, `מִקֶּרֶב` → *from among* — each morpheme has a rendering of its own, the condition is unmet, and rule 2 splits them; what tells the two shapes apart is how many words the ASV wrote and not which senses an English preposition leaves implicit. The corpus fuses `מִפְּנֵי` to *before* in fifteen units and to *because of* in seventy-five, `לִפְנֵי` to *before* in five hundred and ninety-seven, and a preposition with `תּוֹךְ` or `קֶרֶב` to *among* in twenty-seven. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom. **The expression need not be an idiom, and a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme.** Where Hebrew writes a generic head noun before an attributive that names the class — `אִשָּׁה` or `אִישׁ` before a participle or an adjective — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is one unit headed on `זוֹנָה`, with the indefinite article going to that nominal expression under rule 15, and `אִשָּׁה` is not marked `unrepresented` beside it. The one-English-word condition and its subtraction test decide this exactly as they decide a compound preposition — dropping the English word diminishes only the expression as a whole, and no morpheme owns a part of it — so where the ASV instead spends a word on each, as `אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה` → *man of war*, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. Do not read *fixed multi-word Hebrew expression* above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic. **For this rule, a particle's single idiomatic English rendering includes the pronouns the English formula requires.** The entreaty particle `נָא` → *I beseech thee* or *we pray thee* takes the complete formula, headed on *beseech* or *pray*; its English subject and object pronouns are not `added`, because they realize the particle's one entreaty rather than supply arguments of the neighbouring imperative. Where the ASV's formula omits an object, as *I pray*, align only what it writes.
amendments.why: DEU.2.21 marked the `מִן` of `מִפְּנֵיהֶם` `unrepresented` beside a `פָּנֶה` holding the whole of the single word *before*, reasoning from this rule's first sentence that *before* does not carry the ablative sense. That reading contradicts the rule's own fusion sentence, its subtraction test, rule 22's closing paragraph and the corpus, which fuses `מִפְּנֵי` → *before* in fifteen units, `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* in seventy-five, `לִפְנֵי` → *before* in five hundred and ninety-seven and a preposition with `תּוֹךְ` or `קֶרֶב` → *among* in twenty-seven. The rule already named `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* as a fusion and said a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition, but nothing in it said what to do when the single word looks like a rendering of the construct noun alone, and that is the gap a verse pass fell into. The added sentences close it where the over-broad first sentence stands, name the shape that does split (`מִפְּנֵי` → *from before*, `מִקֶּרֶב` → *from among*, both of which this chapter aligns that way), and cite the corpus counts. Nothing else in the rule is altered.

conventions: A preposition standing before `פָּנֶה` is one unit with it wherever the ASV writes a single rendering for the pair — `לְפָנִים` → *aforetime* (2.10, 2.12, 2.20), `לְפָנֵי` → *before* (2.21, 2.31, 2.33, 2.36), `עַל־פְּנֵי` → *upon* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* (2.25) — headed on the construct noun. It is divided, a word to each morpheme, only where the ASV writes two, as `מִפְּנֵי` → *from before* in 2.12 and 2.22. A single *before* written for `מִפְּנֵי` is not evidence that the `מִן` went unrendered, and the preposition is never marked `unrepresented` beside a construct noun holding the whole word.

`נָסַע` rendered *take ... journey* (2.1 *took our journey*, 2.24 *take your journey*) keeps the possessive determiner English writes inside that idiom in the verb's own unit, headed on *journey* under rule 44: no possessive morpheme stands in either clause and English writes no bare *take journey*, so the determiner completes the one rendering rather than supplying a possessor. The competing reading, an `added` pronoun under rule 18's closing sentence, is named in both verses.

report: Read the 66-lemma candidate table and then the whole dump end to end, since the table is blind to `added` units. One real split found: the preposition + `פָּנֶה` compound. DEU.2.10, 2.12 and 2.20 fuse `לְפָנִים` → *aforetime*; 2.31, 2.33 and 2.36 fuse `לְפָנֵי` → *before*; 2.25 fuses `עַל־פְּנֵי` → *upon* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of*. DEU.2.21 alone, on that same one-word shape, marks the `מִן` `unrepresented` and hands the single *before* to `פָּנֶה` — the outcome rule 30 forbids for a fused expression and rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a word. Patched DEU.2.21 to one two-morpheme unit headed on `פָּנֶה`.

DEU.2.12 and DEU.2.22 are not part of that split and were left alone: there the ASV writes *from before*, a word spent on each morpheme, so rule 30's condition is unmet and rule 2 divides them. What separates the two shapes is the English the ASV wrote, and both verses already say so in their notes.

Differences the source or the ASV licenses, checked and left standing: the waw connectives (*And*, *So*, *Then*, *but*, *also*, *with*, *therefore*, *that*, *and when*), each read off the ASV under rules 14, 51 and 55; `עַד` as *until*, *even unto*, *as far as* and *so much as*, and the fused `עַד אֲשֶׁר` → *until* in 2.14 and 2.29; `כִּי` as *for* and *because*; `לְ` unrepresented before `לֵאמֹר` and before a bare English indirect object, against written *to*, *unto*, *that* and *for*; the article counted against each phrase's determiners, so it goes unrepresented wherever a demonstrative carries the one word written (2.3, 2.7, 2.22, 2.25, 2.30, 2.34) and takes the written *the* elsewhere; `מִקֶּרֶב` split in 2.14, 2.15 and 2.16 because the ASV writes a word for each morpheme there.

The three `added` units were re-derived and upheld: *it* (2.24) and *us* (2.37) are object pronouns in clauses that write no object morpheme, which rule 44 leaves `added` rather than folding into the verb; the *and* of *were consumed and dead* (2.16) is a coordinator for a phrase with no conjunction morpheme in it, which rule 14's closing sentence leaves `added` and forbids folding into the `לְ` of `לָמוּת`.

BSB: none of the 33 disagreements is a genuine error. The R × 15 and Td × 13 runs are the documented convention difference — BSB attaches the `לְ` of `לֵאמֹר`, the dative `לְ` and an article the ASV renders by a demonstrative to their host words. The four singletons: the paragogic nun of 2.25 is rule 32; the `בַּ` and `דֶּרֶךְ` of 2.27 are the first half of a doubled phrase the ASV renders once, where rule 22 fixes that one occurrence goes unrepresented but not which, so BSB's choice of the first and ours of the second both satisfy it; the `אֶת` of 2.31 is rule 16; and the waw of 2.36 has no connective written for it, because the ASV's *even unto* is `עַד`'s own compound rendering and rule 16 forbids reading a bare *even* out of it for the waw.
Everything else in the chapter partitions cleanly: 807 units, no missing or duplicated ids, every head a member of its unit. After the patch DEU.2.21 has 22 units instead of 23.
